resources.description: Phoenix HIV/AIDS health and wellness organization (renamed from Southwest Center for HIV/AIDS on Jan. 1, 2025) that people living with HIV/AIDS can contact about housing assistance; the City of Phoenix HOPWA program it is connected to provides short-term rent, mortgage and utility help, move-in costs and housing case management in Maricopa and Pinal counties.
resources.hours: Wellness center (primary care, mental health, social services): Mon–Thu 8 a.m.–7 p.m.; Fri 8 a.m.–3 p.m. Call before visiting — other listings show different hours.
resources.informationText:
**Services Offered**
Prisma Community Care — formerly Southwest Center for HIV/AIDS — is a Phoenix HIV/AIDS health and wellness organization that people living with HIV/AIDS can contact about housing assistance. It is one of the local organizations funded through the City of Phoenix HOPWA (Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS) program. HOPWA housing help in this area includes short-term rent, mortgage and utility payments to stop an eviction, foreclosure or utility shut-off; move-in costs such as security deposits, first and last month's rent, and application fees; and housing case management. Ask specifically about HOPWA housing assistance when you call.

**Eligibility Requirements**
At least one household member must be diagnosed with HIV or AIDS; household income must be at or below 80% of area median income; the household must currently live in Maricopa or Pinal County; and for short-term rent/utility help, the household generally must not already be receiving housing or utility assistance from another housing program. Prisma serves people living with HIV and the wider community; final eligibility for each housing program is decided by the agency administering it.

**Population Served**
People living with or affected by HIV/AIDS and their families, including partners and spouses. The organization also serves 2SLGBTQIA+ people, people of color, and uninsured or underinsured Arizonans. Services are provided in English and Spanish, with interpretation available for other languages.

**How to Best Connect**
Call Prisma at 602-307-5330 (1101 N. Central Ave., Ste. 200, Phoenix; email contactus@prismacare.org) and ask about HOPWA housing assistance. The citywide HOPWA intake is also available: call 602-534-AIDE (602-534-2433), choose option 3, then choose a Family Services Center, then option 3 again to speak with staff — say you are asking about HOPWA. You can also apply online at phoenix.gov/HOPWA. Intake hours are Monday–Friday, 8 a.m.–5 p.m. The office is in downtown Phoenix; plan for a drive or transit trip from Mesa.

**Important Information to Know**
The organization changed its name from Southwest Center for HIV/AIDS on January 1, 2025 — both names mean the same place. Prisma's website highlights medical and wellness services and does not spell out its housing help, so confirm what housing support is currently available for your situation when you call; the citywide HOPWA intake line is the most reliable route to HOPWA housing programs. HOPWA help is grant-funded for eligible households and is not guaranteed — waitlists, appointment availability and funding vary. Published office hours differ slightly between Prisma's website and other directories, so call before visiting. Expect to verify HIV diagnosis, income and county of residence during eligibility screening.
resources.name: Prisma Community Care (formerly Southwest Center for HIV/AIDS) – HIV housing assistance (HOPWA)

resources.address: 2146 E. Apache Blvd., Tempe, AZ 85281 (intake / services site)
resources.description: Rotating overnight emergency shelter for adults experiencing homelessness (men and women), run by Tempe Community Action Agency with faith-community host sites; about 40 spaces with meals, showers, laundry and case management; intakes take place weekday mornings and Mesa's emergency-solutions funding supports this shelter.
resources.hours: I-HELP intake: weekday mornings at 2146 E. Apache Blvd., Tempe — TCAA lists intakes 8–10 a.m.; a 211 record updated April 2026 describes an 8 a.m. first-come waitlist with intakes 10 a.m.–2 p.m.; call first to confirm.
resources.informationText:
**Services Offered**
Overnight emergency shelter for adults experiencing homelessness, operated by Tempe Community Action Agency (TCAA) through a rotating network of faith-community host sites in Tempe. Participants receive a safe sleeping space each night, evening meals, shower and laundry services, and intensive case management and resource navigation aimed at moving from the street to shelter to housing. Daytime resources at TCAA's services site include computers and phones, employment help through TCAA's Financial Success Center, emergency to-go food bags and a hydration station. The shelter serves up to about 40 adults at a time.

**Eligibility Requirements**
Adults (18 and older) who are experiencing homelessness — men and women. Intakes are handled in person on weekday mornings at 2146 E. Apache Blvd., Tempe; call first to confirm the current intake window and process. A City of Mesa resource list notes that I-HELP does not accept individuals with sex-offender status. Whether the Mesa funding contract gives priority to particular households (for example seniors or couples) could not be confirmed — ask staff what is currently being accepted.

**Population Served**
Adults experiencing homelessness in Tempe and the East Valley, including men and women. Mesa's emergency-solutions grant funding supports this shelter for FY 2025/26, and City of Mesa and East Valley shelter lists include it among options for people in the area.

**How to Best Connect**
Call TCAA's I-HELP shelter line at (480) 389-1277 — or the intake-scheduling line at (480) 590-5514 — to check availability, or go to the intake site at 2146 E. Apache Blvd., Tempe, on a weekday morning. Published intake details differ: TCAA's program page lists intakes 8–10 a.m., while a 211 listing updated April 2026 describes arriving at 8 a.m. to get on a first-come waitlist, with intakes between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. Call first to confirm which process is in effect. Space is limited (about 40 adults) and a bed is not guaranteed; 211 notes that no ID or other documents are required for intake. TCAA's services-site front desk is (480) 422-8922, ext. 5882.

**Important Information to Know**
There is no fee to stay in I-HELP (211 lists fees as none). Demand is high — TCAA reports more than 1,000 adults and children experiencing homelessness in Tempe at any given time, while I-HELP assists up to about 40 people at a time — so call early and have a backup plan. TCAA's website lists separate I-HELP shelters in Mesa and Chandler run by other organizations (the Mesa program is for adult women), so if you are in Mesa, ask TCAA which program fits your situation. Host-site schedules, intake rules and bed availability can change; treat this listing as a lead to verify by phone, not a guaranteed place.
resources.name: Tempe Community Action Agency (TCAA) – I-HELP Emergency Shelter
resources.phone: (480) 389-1277 (TCAA I-HELP shelter line); (480) 590-5514 (I-HELP intake scheduling); (480) 422-8922, ext. 5882 (services-site front desk)

resources.description: Chandler Salvation Army center offering emergency financial help that can include short-term rent and utility/energy assistance, plus food boxes and a cooling/heat-relief site; help is limited to the Chandler, Gilbert or Sun Lakes area, funding is not guaranteed, and requests are handled by phone message.
resources.hours: General: Mon–Fri 8:30–11 a.m. and 1–4 p.m. (official page). 211 lists most services 8:30–11:30 a.m. and 1–4:30 p.m.; food boxes Tue–Fri mornings; cooling center daily 11 a.m.–5 p.m.
resources.informationText:
**Services Offered**
Emergency financial assistance for people in crisis — including help with rent payments and utility/energy bills (Project SHARE assistance for SRP and APS customers) — plus emergency food boxes. The site also operates as a cooling center/heat-relief location (listed as Monday–Sunday, 11 a.m.–5 p.m.; hours can vary). This is stabilization help, not shelter: no shelter beds, housing units or motel-voucher program are listed for this location.

**Eligibility Requirements**
People in need who live in the Chandler, Gilbert or Sun Lakes area and who have not received funding from this Salvation Army location in the past 24 months. Funding is limited and not guaranteed even when you qualify, and an application/screening process applies. Mesa households are outside the documented help area — ask about eligibility before applying.

**Population Served**
Individuals and families in financial hardship in the Chandler, Gilbert and Sun Lakes communities. Services are available in English and Spanish.

**How to Best Connect**
Call 480-963-2041 and leave a message about your rent or utility need — this location handles assistance requests by phone message, and staff return calls. You can also visit 85 E. Saragosa St., Chandler, during general hours (Monday–Friday 8:30–11 a.m. and 1–4 p.m.; a separate listing shows service hours of 8:30–11:30 a.m. and 1–4:30 p.m., with food boxes Tuesday–Friday mornings). Call first to confirm you are in the service area and that funds are available.

**Important Information to Know**
There is no fee to apply. Do not promise a motel or shelter voucher through this location: current Salvation Army and 211 listings show rent/utility assistance, food boxes and heat relief, not shelter or motel vouchers — ask when you call in case programs have changed. Assistance is limited and allocated first-come; even eligible households may be turned away when funds run out. Hours and services can change seasonally — verify by phone before going.
resources.name: The Salvation Army – Chandler Corps Community Center – Emergency rent and utility assistance

resources.address: 1500 E. Thomas Rd., Suite 106, Phoenix, AZ 85014
resources.description: VA one-stop center in Phoenix for veterans who are homeless or at risk of homelessness: housing assessments and coordinated-entry referrals for transitional and permanent housing and eviction prevention, plus health care, employment help, benefits and community referrals; walk-in, no referral required, free of charge.
resources.hours: Mon–Fri 7:30 a.m.–4 p.m., excluding federal holidays; walk-in clinic — arrive early for same-day referrals.
resources.informationText:
**Services Offered**
A VA one-stop center for veterans who are homeless or at risk of homelessness. Staff complete housing assessments and refer veterans to transitional housing, permanent housing and eviction-prevention programs, and place eligible veterans on the community-wide housing priority list — this is the veterans' coordinated-entry site for the Phoenix area. The center also helps with immediate food and shelter needs, job training and employment referrals, justice-system navigation and community reentry from jail, financial support to prevent homelessness, addiction and depression treatment, and health and dental care. The National Call Center for Homeless Veterans, 877-424-3838 (877-4AID-VET), answers 24/7.

**Eligibility Requirements**
Veterans who are homeless or at risk of becoming homeless — including veterans transitioning from jail. No referral is required, there is no cost, and you can walk in with or without an appointment. Bring identification and any military/VA paperwork you have; some on-site health services require VA eligibility or enrollment in a VA homeless program.

**Population Served**
Veterans and veteran families experiencing homelessness or housing instability in Maricopa County, including veterans leaving jail or prison.

**How to Best Connect**
Walk in or call: 1500 E. Thomas Rd., Suite 106, Phoenix, AZ 85014; phone 602-248-6040; email VHAPHOCRRCStaff@va.gov. Open Monday–Friday, 7:30 a.m.–4 p.m., closed federal holidays. It is a walk-in clinic, so arrive as early in the day as possible — same-day referrals, including to transitional housing, may not be possible if you arrive late in the afternoon; if that happens, staff can still provide community shelter referrals. After hours, call 877-424-3838.

**Important Information to Know**
The center is in central Phoenix — plan your transportation from Mesa. No referral is needed to walk in and ask for help, and services are free of charge. A housing assessment is not an immediate placement: referrals depend on program capacity and the community priority list, so timelines vary. Veterans who also need health, mental-health, benefits or employment help can often start those services during the same visit.
resources.name: VA Community Resource & Referral Center (CRRC) – Phoenix (veteran housing and coordinated entry)
resources.phone: 602-248-6040; 877-424-3838 (24/7 National Call Center for Homeless Veterans)

resources.address: 1500 E. Thomas Rd., Suite 106, Phoenix, AZ 85014 (Phoenix VA Community Resource & Referral Center — walk-in veteran access point)
resources.description: HUD-VASH pairs a HUD Housing Choice Voucher (rental assistance for a private-market apartment or home) with VA case management and supportive services so veterans experiencing homelessness can move into and stay in permanent housing. Veterans connect through VA — the Phoenix VA Community Resource and Referral Center (602-248-6040, walk-in) or the National Call Center for Homeless Veterans (877-424-3838, 24/7).
resources.hours: Walk-in access at the Phoenix VA Community Resource and Referral Center: Monday–Friday 7:30 a.m.–4:00 p.m. (excluding federal holidays); arrive early for same-day referrals. The National Call Center for Homeless Veterans phone line is answered 24/7.
resources.informationText:
**Services Offered**
Permanent supportive housing for veterans: a HUD Housing Choice Voucher that pays part of the rent for a qualifying privately owned apartment or house, paired with ongoing VA case management and clinical support — including connection to primary care, mental health care and substance-use treatment, help with budgeting and leases, and long-term support to remain housed. Vouchers are administered locally by public housing authorities in partnership with VA, and the Phoenix VA homeless programs team handles referrals for Mesa and Maricopa County veterans.

**Eligibility Requirements**
For veterans who are experiencing homelessness and need ongoing, intensive case management (for example, due to chronic health conditions or other complex challenges). Veterans must be eligible for VA health care and meet HUD-VASH income limits — as of HUD's 2024 policy change, initial income eligibility is set at the Low level (80% of area median income) for all housing agencies, and service-connected disability benefits are not counted when determining income eligibility. A referral through VA is required; veterans cannot get a HUD-VASH voucher directly from a housing authority. Veterans who do not need intensive case management are usually served through other VA or community programs.

**Population Served**
Veterans — including veterans with families — who are experiencing homelessness in the Phoenix VA catchment area, which includes Mesa and Maricopa County.

**How to Best Connect**
Call or walk in to the Phoenix VA Community Resource and Referral Center (CRRC): 1500 E. Thomas Rd., Suite 106, Phoenix, AZ 85014; phone 602-248-6040; email VHAPHOCRRCStaff@va.gov. Hours are Monday–Friday 7:30 a.m.–4:00 p.m., excluding federal holidays. It is a walk-in clinic, so arrive as early as possible for a same-day referral (very late arrivals may instead receive a community shelter referral). Veterans can also call the National Call Center for Homeless Veterans at 877-424-3838 (free, confidential, 24/7) or ask their VA primary care team or social worker for a HUD-VASH referral.

**Important Information to Know**
Cost: the voucher pays the portion of rent above what the veteran contributes — generally about 30% of adjusted monthly income; utility allowances can adjust that amount. A referral does not guarantee a voucher, an available unit, or a timeline — voucher and case-manager capacity are limited, and the veteran must find a landlord who accepts the voucher; ask about current local availability when you call. HUD-VASH is separate from the regular Section 8 waiting list (Phoenix's regular Housing Choice Voucher list is currently closed); the City of Phoenix Housing Department administers HUD-VASH vouchers with the VA (about 903 vouchers awarded), and referrals still come through the VA, not the city.
resources.name: HUD-VASH (HUD-VA Supportive Housing) — VA Phoenix Health Care System
resources.phone: 602-248-6040 (Phoenix VA Community Resource & Referral Center); 877-424-3838 (National Call Center for Homeless Veterans, 24/7)

resources.address: 3507 N. Central Ave., Suite 200, Phoenix, AZ 85012 (offices); residential campus: M.D. Hawkins Veterans Center, 12027 N. 28th Dr., Phoenix, AZ 85029
resources.description: U.S.VETS Phoenix provides housing and wraparound services for veterans in Maricopa County: transitional housing for veterans experiencing homelessness, on-site permanent supportive housing, and SSVF help (rapid re-housing, rent and security-deposit assistance, eviction prevention) for very low-income veteran families — plus mental health counseling, career services and case management. Veterans seeking housing should contact the outreach team.
resources.hours: Supportive Services for Veteran Families: Monday–Friday 7 a.m.–4 p.m. and by appointment; aftercare: 9 a.m.–5 p.m.; residential campus open 24/7; case management by appointment. Call before visiting — hours vary by program.
resources.informationText:
**Services Offered**
Transitional housing for veterans experiencing homelessness with wraparound support (case management, life skills, counseling, career training, VA benefits assistance); on-site permanent supportive housing where veterans can take over the lease; SSVF (Supportive Services for Veteran Families) rapid re-housing and homelessness-prevention help, including rent payments, security deposits, moving costs and transportation; free mental health and substance-use counseling; employment and career services; aftercare case management after a veteran moves into permanent housing. Housing campuses include the M.D. Hawkins Veterans Center (opened 2026, with a dedicated wing for women veterans) and Ashley's Place, a transitional housing program for women veterans.

**Eligibility Requirements**
Veteran who served in the active military, naval service or Coast Guard with a discharge other than dishonorable; must be homeless or at imminent risk of losing housing; very low income for most services. Permanent housing programming is aimed at veterans who can live independently and are economically self-sufficient. Ashley's Place serves women veterans who experienced military sexual trauma, intimate partner violence or domestic violence during or after service and who can live independently in a shared housing environment; eligibility screening applies. Typical documents: photo ID, DD Form 214 (or letter of service) showing discharge status, recent proof of household income, proof of homelessness (or current lease and eviction notice if housed), and Social Security cards for household members.

**Population Served**
Veterans in Maricopa County, including women veterans and veteran families. U.S.VETS Phoenix reports it supports more than 300 veterans experiencing homelessness every day and has served more than 10,000 veterans since opening in 2001.

**How to Best Connect**
For transitional housing, call the outreach team at 602-757-9723 or 602-859-7329. For SSVF and family housing help, call 602-441-0612. Main line: 602-717-6682. Offices: 3507 N. Central Ave., Suite 200, Phoenix, AZ 85012; residential campus: M.D. Hawkins Veterans Center, 12027 N. 28th Dr., Phoenix, AZ 85029. Calling, emailing or visiting the office starts the process; veterans working with VA can ask their VA case manager to refer them. Hours: SSVF Monday–Friday 7 a.m.–4 p.m. and by appointment; aftercare 9 a.m.–5 p.m.; residential site open 24/7; case management by appointment.

**Important Information to Know**
Most services are free; transitional housing fees vary. Program openings, beds and screening outcomes are limited — call ahead to confirm current availability, and do not count on immediate placement. Some programs serve specific groups (Ashley's Place: women veterans; SSVF: very low-income veteran households). Hours and program details differ by service and can change; confirm by phone before traveling.
resources.name: U.S.VETS Phoenix — veteran housing and supportive services
resources.phone: 602-717-6682 (main); 602-757-9723 or 602-859-7329 (housing outreach team); 602-441-0612 (Supportive Services for Veteran Families)

resources.address: 3307 E. Van Buren St., Phoenix, AZ 85008 (call before visiting)
resources.description: The Family Housing Hub is the single front door for families with children under 18 who are homeless or at risk of homelessness in Maricopa County. Families call for an assessment, a housing plan, diversion help, and referral to family emergency shelter and housing programs — including rapid re-housing, transitional and permanent supportive housing. Mesa families can use this route; 2-1-1 is the recommended first call.
resources.hours: Call to confirm — posted hours differ between sources: a current 211 Arizona listing shows Monday 1–6 p.m. and Tuesday–Friday 10 a.m.–3 p.m.; earlier notices list Monday 8 a.m.–7 p.m., Tuesday–Thursday 8 a.m.–4 p.m. and Friday 10 a.m.–4 p.m.
resources.informationText:
**Services Offered**
Coordinated entry and assessment for families with children under 18 who are experiencing or at risk of homelessness in Maricopa County: connection to family emergency shelter (including placement on the family shelter waiting list), diversion help that can resolve a housing crisis without entering shelter when possible, a short- and long-term housing plan, and referrals to rapid re-housing, transitional housing and permanent supportive housing programs. The Hub also connects families to other community resources (food, benefits, employment, health care) and serves families that include a military veteran.

**Eligibility Requirements**
Families with children under 18 who are homeless or at risk of homelessness. Families should call (602) 595-8700 before going in person, and all adults 18+ in the household are required to take part in the call or visit. An assessment does not guarantee shelter or a housing voucher — referrals depend on eligibility and limited availability.

**Population Served**
Families with dependent children under 18 in Maricopa County, including Mesa. Help is available in English and Spanish.

**How to Best Connect**
Call (602) 595-8700, or dial 2-1-1 (877-211-8661). UMOM recommends calling 2-1-1 or checking 211arizona.org before visiting to get matched with the best resources for your family, including options that may prevent homelessness. Location: 3307 E. Van Buren St., Phoenix, AZ 85008 (near the UMOM campus); program website: fhhub.org. Families already on the list use the Hub's check-in number for weekly check-ins. Confirm hours by phone before traveling — published hours differ between sources.

**Important Information to Know**
There is no fee. Wait times are the main challenge: in September 2026, more than 200 families were on the family shelter waitlist with waits described as about three months (Mesa has cited 2–4 month coordinated-entry waits); ask about diversion, rapid re-housing referrals and 2-1-1 options while you wait. Earlier community guides listed Mesa-area entry points (Mesa CAN at 635 E. Broadway and Save the Family at 125 E. University Dr.) on certain weekdays, but later notices said the East Valley and West Valley sites were closed and families should call the main line — confirm current options by phone. If the fhhub.org website does not load, call (602) 595-8700 directly.

resources.description: A seasonal, referral-based heat-relief program run by UMOM with the City of Phoenix for families with minor children experiencing homelessness: daytime and overnight shelter (including indoor tent and cot space) on UMOM's Phoenix campus, plus hotel stays used as overflow when respite space is full. Families get help through the family homeless-services system — call 2-1-1 or the Family Housing Hub (602-595-8700).
resources.hours: Seasonal heat-season program; the 2026 City of Phoenix contract runs through October 31, 2026, and UMOM reported extending heat relief through the end of October 2026. The heat relief site operated 24/7 (daytime and overnight) during the season. No direct public intake — access is by referral.
resources.informationText:
**Services Offered**
Heat-relief respite for families with minor children experiencing homelessness: a 24/7 space with daytime and overnight shelter (including cots in indoor tents — 16 tents were added as the site filled up), meals and staff support, operated on UMOM's Phoenix campus during the extreme-heat season. UMOM also assesses each family for diversion and shelters those who cannot be diverted, and provides hotel stays as overflow when respite capacity is full. By late August 2026, UMOM reported serving 757 people, including 449 children (data as of Aug. 25), with expectations of more than 1,000 people served before the season ended; the city reported more than twice as many families served this year as in all of summer 2025.

**Eligibility Requirements**
Families with minor children who are experiencing homelessness. Access is by referral — the City of Phoenix contract specifies referrals from other heat relief sites and City of Phoenix outreach workers; there is no public application or walk-up intake for the hotel stays. Families should be assessed through the family homeless-services system (call 2-1-1 or the Family Housing Hub).

**Population Served**
Families with minor children experiencing homelessness in Phoenix and the surrounding Maricopa County area. UMOM is the region's family coordinated entry provider and the state's largest family shelter provider.

**How to Best Connect**
There is no direct intake line for this program — referrals come through heat relief sites and City of Phoenix outreach teams, and UMOM's own guidance for families in a housing crisis is to call 2-1-1. Families with children can also call the Family Housing Hub at 602-595-8700 for assessment and shelter referral. UMOM main line: 602-275-7852; campus: 3333 E. Van Buren St., Phoenix, AZ 85008. Ask specifically about summer heat relief and family shelter availability when you call.

**Important Information to Know**
This is a seasonal program tied to the heat season, and 2026 availability is time-limited — the City of Phoenix contract runs through October 31, 2026, and UMOM reported extending heat relief through the end of October 2026. Capacity has been under heavy strain: in September 2026, some families with hotel stays were reportedly told to check out earlier than planned — ahead of a reported Sept. 30 end date for the hotel portion — while UMOM looked into the cause, so treat hotel availability as limited and confirm at the time of need. The service is city-funded; no family fees are described in the contract. Outside the heat season, use 2-1-1 and the Family Housing Hub for year-round family shelter and housing help.

resources.description: UMOM's New Day Center family emergency shelter provides safe temporary shelter and intensive support for households with children experiencing homelessness in Maricopa County. Families are screened through the UMOM-operated Family Housing Hub, the countywide coordinated entry point for families; the campus provides private rooms, meals, case management, employment services, children's programs and help moving to permanent housing.

UMOM's main line is staffed Mon-Fri 8 a.m.-5 p.m.; a city resource listing also describes the UMOM campus as open daily 8 a.m.-5 p.m. for resource access, with intake/waitlist handled by phone.
resources.informationText:
**Services Offered**

Emergency shelter on the UMOM New Day Center campus for households with children. Families receive private rooms; fresh meals served 7 days a week; one-on-one case management; employment services and job training (including UMOM's Homegrown culinary and warehouse/logistics tracks); help connecting to benefits such as WIC and unemployment; advocacy with property managers, landlords and courts; connections to community resources; help finding permanent housing, including housing vouchers when available; rapid rehousing and permanent affordable/supportive housing pathways after shelter; on-site children's services, including an on-site Boys & Girls Club and a children's health clinic run by Phoenix Children's Hospital; adult health care through partners (Health Care for the Homeless and Circle the City); and daily school bus service that keeps children in their home school.

**Eligibility Requirements**

Families with dependent children (children under 18) who are experiencing homelessness in Maricopa County. Families are screened, prioritized and placed on the shelter waitlist through the Family Housing Hub, the single countywide coordinated entry point for families, rather than applying directly at the shelter. Families that include a veteran can also access support through the Family Housing Hub on the UMOM campus.

**Population Served**

Families with children experiencing homelessness in Maricopa County, including larger families (a 2022-2024 county-funded expansion targeted families averaging six members) and families with non-traditional heads of household. UMOM reports serving about 75% of families in Maricopa County shelters and sheltering roughly 155 families (about 800 people) on campus each night.

**How to Best Connect**

Start with the Family Housing Hub: call or text 2-1-1, or call 602-595-8700 (also 877-211-8661); online at fhhub.org. UMOM asks families to call 2-1-1 or visit 211arizona.org before going in person so they are matched with the best options, which may include help to avoid shelter. The Family Housing Hub is at 3307 E. Van Buren St. #108, Phoenix, AZ 85008, next to the UMOM campus at 3333 E. Van Buren St.; intake is handled by phone and English/Spanish are available there. UMOM's main line is 602-275-7852. Confirm current hours and any in-person arrangements before sending a family.

**Important Information to Know**

No fees are charged (211 lists no fees for the shelter or the Hub). Placement is not immediate: UMOM manages the single countywide family shelter waitlist and reported in mid-2026 that more than 200 families were experiencing homelessness and in need of shelter; capacity and waitlist status change daily. Length of stay varies - recent UMOM participant materials describe a short-term emergency shelter stay (30 days) focused on diversion and housing search, while older materials cite stays of up to 120 days - so confirm current terms at intake. Shelter is a step toward permanent housing; a 2024 county case study reported 802 individuals moved into permanent housing from the program that year.

resources.description: UMOM's Halle Women's Center is an emergency shelter in Phoenix for single women age 18 and older who are experiencing homelessness in Maricopa County, including women fleeing domestic violence. Women call the intake line to get onto the shelter waiting list, then receive meals, case management, employment support and help finding permanent housing.
resources.hours: Call 602-362-5833 for intake and the waiting list. Reported intake hours 6 a.m.-2:30 p.m.; administration Mon-Fri 8 a.m.-5 p.m.; the shelter operates 24/7 (per a current 211 listing, last assured 04/01/2026).
resources.informationText:
**Services Offered**

Emergency shelter specifically for single women, with rooms shared by two or three women and private bathrooms. Residents receive fresh meals served daily; one-on-one case management; employment services to help secure and keep a job; advocacy with property managers, landlords, courts and partner agencies; connections to community resources; and help with the search for permanent housing. The center serves up to about 130 women each night and is designed for single women without children.

**Eligibility Requirements**

Single women age 18 and older who are experiencing homelessness; no children in their care for this program (women with children go through the Family Housing Hub instead). Victims of domestic violence are explicitly included, but the shelter is not limited to domestic-violence survivors. There is always a waiting list for shelter.

**Population Served**

Single adult women experiencing homelessness in Maricopa County, including survivors of domestic violence. UMOM describes Halle as the first shelter in Arizona designed specifically for single women.

**How to Best Connect**

Call the Halle Women's Center intake line at 602-362-5833 to get onto the waiting list for shelter. Reported intake hours are 6 a.m.-2:30 p.m.; one city shelter list advises calling at 6:30 a.m. on weekdays for the intake prescreen - confirm the current intake window by phone. Administration is Mon-Fri 8 a.m.-5 p.m.; the shelter operates 24/7. Location: 3424 E. Van Buren St., Phoenix, AZ 85008, across the street from the UMOM main campus (3333 E. Van Buren St.). UMOM's main line is 602-275-7852; program information is at umom.org/find-help.

**Important Information to Know**

No fees are charged (211 lists none). A bed is not guaranteed: there is always a waiting list and availability changes daily. A 211 listing marks the exact shelter location as confidential even though UMOM publishes the street address - call before going. For women who need a confidential domestic-violence placement, UMOM currently lists DVSTOP (A New Leaf) at 480-890-3039 / 844-SAFE-DVS, described as short-term emergency placement when Maricopa County domestic-violence shelters are full. There is a conflict to be aware of: Maricopa County's and the Continuum of Care's pages still list that number as the 24-hour 'SAFEDVS' hotline, while 2026 reporting says the former countywide SAFEDVS centralized line stopped full service on May 15, 2026 and now directs callers to shelters directly - confirm what the line currently handles when you call. Additional 24-hour routes: National Domestic Violence Hotline 800-799-7233; ArizonaSurvivors.org lists current Maricopa shelter options. Women with children should be routed through the Family Housing Hub instead.
resources.name: UMOM Halle Women's Center

resources.description: A Maricopa County lead for youth shelter and independent living services that were historically operated by UMOM after it absorbed Tumbleweed's youth programs in 2017: a crisis shelter for unaccompanied minors ages 12-17 and independent living programs for youth ages 16-21. The current operator of the attributed programs is unresolved - UMOM's current program pages describe shelter for families and single women, while Child Crisis Arizona adopted the Independent Living Program effective July 1, 2021 and operates Maricopa County's Safe Place youth crisis program. For immediate help for a youth 12-17, call Safe Place at 602-841-5799.
resources.hours: Not established - the current operator and hours for the youth crisis shelter and independent living services are unresolved. For youth 12-17 in crisis, the Safe Place line 602-841-5799 is available 24/7.
resources.informationText:
**Services Offered**

Historically, this included a youth crisis shelter in Maricopa County for unaccompanied minors ages 12-17 (known as Open Hands under UMOM/Tumbleweed), providing shelter, food, counseling, education support and family reunification, with longer stays and life/workforce skills for youth who could not return home; and independent living programs for youth ages 16-21 (including young parents with minor children) providing housing, case management, counseling, life skills and transportation help. It is not confirmed that UMOM still operates these programs: the Independent Living Program was adopted by Child Crisis Arizona effective July 1, 2021 - serving up to about 50 youth ages 16-21 at two Phoenix locations, with several beds reserved for youth who reach the Safe Place program - and Child Crisis Arizona is the documented operator of Maricopa County's Safe Place youth crisis response (ages 12-17).

**Eligibility Requirements**

As historically described: unaccompanied minor youth ages 12-17 for the crisis shelter (a legal guardian must be located within 24 hours of entering shelter), and youth ages 16-21, including those with minor children, for independent living/transitional programs. Current eligibility must be confirmed with the operating agency before any referral - the independent living program now primarily serves youth in or aging out of foster care (with Safe Place beds included), and Safe Place serves any youth 12-17 who needs help.

**Population Served**

Youth experiencing homelessness, runaways and youth in family conflict or unsafe situations (ages 12-17), and transition-age youth preparing for independence, including youth aging out of foster care (ages 16-21) - based on the historical program descriptions for these services.

**How to Best Connect**

For immediate safety and shelter for a youth 12-17 anywhere in Maricopa County, call or text Safe Place: 602-841-5799, or text 'SAFE' plus the youth's location to 4HELP (44357). Safe Place sites include all QuikTrip and Valley Metro locations. To ask whether UMOM still operates any youth crisis shelter or independent living services, call UMOM's main line at 602-275-7852. Child Crisis Arizona (childcrisisaz.org) is the documented current operator of both the former UMOM Independent Living Program and Safe Place. Do not send a youth to the former UMOM/Open Hands youth shelter address without confirming who currently operates it.

**Important Information to Know**

Current operator unresolved: UMOM's current program pages describe shelter for families and single women, and no youth shelter or independent living program appears among them. In 2021 the Youth Independent Living Program moved from UMOM to Child Crisis Arizona (effective July 1, 2021), and Child Crisis Arizona announced it became the home of Safe Place in Maricopa County (the 12-17 crisis line above); several Child Crisis Arizona beds are reserved for youth who reach Safe Place overnight. Some older profiles and directories still attribute a 12-17 youth crisis shelter (Open Hands; one directory describes a six-bed shelter serving about 200 youth a year) and the 16-21 independent living program to UMOM, and reported bed counts differ (6 vs. 10). Because a misdirected referral could put a minor at risk, treat this as a lead to verify, not a confirmed placement route; the Safe Place line is the supported current entry point for youth 12-17.
resources.name: UMOM/Tumbleweed Youth Crisis Shelter and Independent Living Programs (ages 12-17; 16-21)
resources.phone: 602-275-7852 (UMOM main line); 602-841-5799 (Safe Place, 24/7 youth crisis line)
resources.resolutionReason: Consequential unresolved attribution: UMOM's current program materials list shelter for families and single women; child-welfare and youth-service announcements document that the Independent Living Program was adopted by Child Crisis Arizona effective July 1, 2021 (up to about 50 youth ages 16-21 at two Phoenix locations, some beds reserved for Safe Place youth) and that Child Crisis Arizona operates the county's Safe Place youth crisis response - while older UMOM profiles and directories still attribute a 12-17 youth crisis shelter (Open Hands) and the 16-21 program to UMOM, with conflicting bed counts. No current UMOM-operated youth shelter or independent living program could be confirmed, so a referral to a 'UMOM youth shelter' cannot be responsibly made; the Safe Place line (602-841-5799; text SAFE + location to 44357) is the supported live route for a youth 12-17 in immediate crisis, and the historical lead is retained for administrator verification and reconciliation of older listings.

resources.description: UMOM's youth outreach team is a coordinated-entry access point for young adults ages 18-24 experiencing homelessness in Maricopa County, combining street outreach with a youth resource day center. Young adults can get food, water, showers, hygiene items and clothing, case management, a housing assessment, housing navigation, and connection to HUD housing programs such as rapid rehousing and permanent supportive housing. Call 480-868-7527.
resources.hours: Reported drop-in/resource hours: Mon-Fri 12-3:30 p.m. (older listings; confirm by phone). The outreach team also works on the street, including evenings.
resources.informationText:
**Services Offered**

Free supportive services for young adults ages 18-24 experiencing homelessness: street outreach to youth on the streets; a walk-in resource/day center with food and water, showers, hygiene and personal care items, clothing, and a food box; case management; housing navigation and housing assessments; coordinated entry (a direct access point, not just a directory listing) for HUD housing programs including rapid rehousing and permanent supportive housing; and connections to education, employment and medical care (earlier listings offered free medical visits at the day site through Phoenix Children's Hospital's Healthmobile).

**Eligibility Requirements**

Young adults ages 18-24 who are experiencing homelessness or housing instability in Maricopa County. Housing programs are accessed by completing a housing assessment (TAY-VI-SPDAT) through coordinated entry; resource-center services are described as free and low-barrier.

**Population Served**

Young adults ages 18-24 experiencing homelessness in Maricopa County, including street-based youth; the day center historically also welcomed teens as young as 12 with its outreach services.

**How to Best Connect**

Call 480-868-7527 to reach UMOM's youth outreach/coordinated-entry line for ages 18-24. The youth access/day center has been listed at Tempe First United Methodist Church, 215 E. University Drive, Tempe, AZ 85281, with reported drop-in hours of Mon-Fri 12-3:30 p.m.; some older listings give the UMOM campus at 3333 E. Van Buren St. in Phoenix. A current community listing also gives 602-819-9361 for the youth (18-24) access point at the Tempe address. Confirm the current location, hours and intake steps by phone before sending a client - the outreach team also meets youth where they are.

**Important Information to Know**

This program is not currently described on UMOM's main website, so verify by phone before relying on it. Listings conflict on the day-center address and hours; 480-868-7527 is the most consistently published contact. The Maricopa Regional CoC's current Get Help page routes youth 18-24 to a county Youth Resource Guide for access instructions rather than naming this number directly, so confirm current coverage by phone. Services are free; housing program openings depend on the housing assessment and available capacity/waitlists, and nothing is guaranteed. For youth under 18 in crisis, call Safe Place at 602-841-5799.
resources.name: UMOM Youth Outreach (ages 18-24)

starterSets.gaps: No confirmed emergency shelter capacity for young adults 18-24 in Mesa/East Valley: the UMOM youth records are unconfirmed or historical (operator transferred to Child Crisis Arizona), Covenant House has no Arizona site, and only Safe Place (12-17) plus outreach/coordinated-entry points (NAC; UMOM youth outreach) are verified.; No general hotel/motel voucher program and no safe-parking pathway: Red Cross assistance is disaster-triggered, UMOM heat relief is seasonal and referral-based, and hotel-based shelters (Off the Streets, Sue's Espacio, Rio Fresco) are referral-only.; Reentry housing: no confirmed community-referral reentry beds in Phoenix (Dismas' Phoenix facility unconfirmed); H2O and HUD-VASH touch reentry but require health-plan or VA routes.; No open voucher waitlists captured: Mesa HCV, HAMC, Tempe and Phoenix lists are closed or referral-only - no immediate Section 8 application pathway.; Mesa I-HELP rotating shelter unresolved - no confirmed rotating-shelter intake for Mesa adults (operator largely resolved to LSS-SW serving adult women, current operation unconfirmed).; Eviction/tenant legal defense is not represented as a resource (AZEvictionHelp.org appears only as a referral mention).; East Valley single-women capacity: no confirmed Mesa-area beds for women without children; Halle Women's Center (Phoenix) and DV shelters are the closest options.; No confirmed women-veterans-specific beds in Maricopa County (MANA House described for male veterans; Ashley's Place within U.S.VETS noted but not separately verified).

members.limitation: No phone intakes; beds via waitlist and availability can change daily; children under 18 are not allowed on site.

members.contribution: Mesa's rent/utility crisis window with a Spanish application path, documented criteria and a clear document list.
members.limitation: Mesa residents only; first-come funding with narrow appointment windows (first-Thursday rent line, limited slots).

members.contribution: The rental-subsidy rehousing route (up to 12 months plus move-in help and case management) that shows clients what coordinated entry can lead to beyond shelter.
members.limitation: No direct applications - entry only through coordinated entry (211); funding and timing vary.

members.contribution: The East Valley's local DV shelter - 22 beds, any gender, pet-friendly, screened through A New Leaf's 24-hour hotline.
members.limitation: Confidential location; placement not guaranteed; the May 2026 countywide DV hotline transition means confirming the current intake route.

members.contribution: The 12-17 crisis entry - call, text or walk into Safe Place sites (QuikTrip, Valley Metro, libraries, fire stations) for immediate youth help countywide.
members.limitation: Overnight shelter not guaranteed; use the current 44357 text instructions (older guides show 69866).

members.contribution: The veterans' walk-in front door - housing assessments and referrals (transitional, permanent, eviction prevention), the HUD-VASH pathway, benefits and health care, free of charge.
members.limitation: Weekdays 7:30 a.m.-4 p.m.; central Phoenix; referrals depend on capacity - arrive early for same-day referrals.

starterSets.rationale: Ten complementary usable starters spanning distinct pathways: statewide navigation (211), the single-adult and family coordinated-entry front doors, Mesa's shelter for families/women/seniors, Mesa's men's shelter, Mesa's rent/utility crisis aid, the rental-subsidy rehousing route, the East Valley DV shelter, the 12-17 youth crisis line, and the veterans' walk-in access point. The set deliberately mixes service types - navigation, entry/assessment, shelter, financial aid, rehousing, safety, youth, veterans - rather than several variants of one service, and each limitation is stated so missionaries can set expectations before calling. All needs-resolution records (Helaman House, SAFEDVS, the tracker, UMOM youth crisis/ILP, NREC, Dismas, the Resource Village, Mesa I-HELP) remain outside the starter set with administrator-focused reasons, and reserve usable resources (deposit help, the Mesa Resource Line, second DV shelters, Vista Colina, HUD-VASH, AHP/H2O, DDD lanes, additional shelter capacity) carry considerations written against this actual set. No tiers or reserve ranks are introduced.

forGroups.definition: A service designed for a household, parent-child unit, kinship family or family supporters. A family-law case alone does not establish a family-service program.
forGroups.label: Families

forGroups.definition: Adults without children in their care, including single men and women.
forGroups.label: Single adults

forGroups.definition: A dedicated women’s program or women-specific health, housing or support pathway. A name or a condition affecting all genders does not establish this group.
forGroups.label: Women

forGroups.definition: A dedicated men’s program, men’s housing or father-specific pathway. A general service admitting adults does not qualify solely because men may participate.
forGroups.label: Men

forGroups.definition: A dedicated older-adult program, age-based benefit or specific older-adult access pathway. A general service available across all ages does not qualify solely because it mentions older adults.
forGroups.label: Seniors

forGroups.definition: A dedicated military-service, veteran or eligible military-household pathway. Service, discharge and program rules differ.
forGroups.label: Veterans

forGroups.definition: A child, adolescent or explicitly youth-targeted young-adult pathway. Program ages vary; a general adult service is not tagged merely because some young adults could use it.
forGroups.label: Youth

forGroups.definition: A dedicated domestic/intimate-partner abuse safety, shelter, advocacy, legal or recovery pathway. Other uses of the word survivor do not qualify.
forGroups.label: Domestic violence survivors

forGroups.definition: A program specifically addressing homelessness, unsheltered living or imminent housing loss. Poverty, food need or ordinary rental assistance alone does not establish this pathway.
forGroups.label: Homeless

forGroups.definition: A disability-targeted program, eligibility route or documented disability accommodation. Diagnosis or participation in health care alone does not qualify. Includes the more specific vision and hearing groups.
forGroups.label: People with disabilities

forGroups.definition: People with serious mental illness or high-need mental health/substance use conditions.
forGroups.label: People with behavioral health needs

forGroups.definition: Households with at least one member diagnosed with HIV or AIDS.
forGroups.label: People living with HIV/AIDS

forGroups.definition: People maintaining sobriety from alcohol or other drugs who need recovery-supportive housing.
forGroups.label: People in substance-use recovery

forGroups.definition: A service explicitly targeted to people preparing for release, returning from custody, under justice supervision or addressing a criminal-record barrier. Prior incarceration is not required for every included program.
forGroups.label: Re-entry

forGroups.definition: A dedicated condition, recovery, medical-equipment or clinically vulnerable access pathway such as cancer rides, NICU support or medical respite. General patients or all Medicaid members do not automatically qualify.
forGroups.label: Medically vulnerable

forGroups.definition: Explicit Spanish-language service, interpretation, staff or program access. This describes language access and does not imply ethnicity or immigration status.
forGroups.label: Spanish

forGroups.definition: A documented pet-accommodation, pet-supply or pet-related access pathway. This does not promise that every animal or shelter placement is accepted.
forGroups.label: Pet owners

forGroups.definition: A tribal-member-specific or explicitly Native/urban-Indian culturally focused program. Tribal-land benefit geography alone does not establish identity-based eligibility; culturally focused programs may also welcome other clients.
forGroups.label: Native American

types.definition: Short-term crisis shelter and direct coordinated shelter-entry routes.
types.label: Emergency shelter

types.definition: Time-limited housing with a plan toward longer-term stability.
types.label: Transitional housing

types.definition: Longer-term housing paired with ongoing support services.
types.label: Supportive housing

types.definition: Rental subsidies, homelessness prevention, rapid rehousing or move-in/deposit assistance with programme-specific eligibility.
types.label: Rent and deposit help

types.definition: One-time or short-term financial help with rent, mortgage, utility bills or move-in deposits to prevent eviction or shut-off, or to enable a move into housing.
types.label: Rent, utility & deposit crisis assistance

types.definition: Housing Choice Vouchers, project-based and special-purpose vouchers (VASH, Mainstream, EHV, TBRA) administered by housing authorities; access is usually waitlist- or referral-based.
types.label: Housing vouchers & subsidized rent programs

types.definition: Income-restricted apartment or home communities owned or managed by nonprofits, agencies or authorities, with applications handled at the property or portfolio level.
types.label: Affordable housing communities

types.definition: Staffed sites or lines where people complete a housing assessment and are routed to shelter and housing programs - the region's front doors, including population-specific routes.
types.label: Coordinated entry & housing access points

types.definition: Help finding housing, assessment, application support or outreach connecting people to housing; not a promise of a unit.
types.label: Housing navigation

types.definition: Mobile teams and request lines that engage people living unsheltered, provide supplies and case management, and connect them to shelter, housing and services.
types.label: Street outreach & mobile services

types.definition: Sober living or residential recovery programmes; treatment and house requirements are stated separately.
types.label: Recovery housing

types.definition: Housing or lodging support tied to a specific health condition - medical respite while recovering from illness or injury, and HOPWA housing assistance for people living with HIV/AIDS.
types.label: Health-linked housing (respite & HIV/AIDS)

types.definition: Temporary animal care and assistance that remove pet-related barriers to housing or shelter.
types.label: Pet housing support

types.definition: Crisis shelter, group-home care and crisis access for minors and young people - children's shelters, teen group homes, youth crisis lines and safe-site networks.
types.label: Children & youth crisis care
